The Sappho–Catullus comparison is well-trodden: Higgins ("Sappho's Splintered Tongue," *AJP* 111.2, 1990), Radenković & Maričić (2018), Greene (*Re-Reading Sappho*, 1996), duBois (*Sappho Is Burning*, 1995). claims.statement: The erratum, once published, will enter the transmission grammar itself. It will be the text in which the claim is preserved under the sign of its retraction. Future readers who know the claim only through the erratum will know it as *the claim that was withdrawn*, and the withdrawal will be the means by which the claim survives. This is not a hypothesis. It is the grammar's own law: retraction is the most durable form of transmission, because a retracted claim is a claim that has been judged worthy of the labour of retraction, and the labour is copied, and the copying is the survival. The erratum would therefore not merely fail to withdraw the claim; it would *canonize* it.
